11545-travels-in-the-united-states-of-am:
William Priest, a musician late of the theatres of Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Boston, published his travels in London in 1802. The book covers 1793 to 1797, with journals of two Atlantic voyages added. He wrote the work on his return in 1797 for friends, and resisted publishing it for years.

He feared, with a joke, that a preface might only put readers to sleep, and that his book would not much affect the price of opium. The volume mixes travel notes with songs and poems, among them verses on a shepherd who leaves the forest for native shades and is welcomed back by Indians. It gives a theatre man's view of the young republic.
12694-history-of-the-american-clock-busi:
Chauncey Jerome wrote this 1860 memoir-history of the American clock trade from his own long career in Connecticut. He traces the shift from wooden works, made slowly by a few men with plain tools, to brass movements turned out by large factories. Exports, southern markets, and the panic of 1837 all shape the story.

Jerome names makers, firms, and rivals, and tells how firms rose and fell, some closing after making thousands of clocks a year. P. T. Barnum's link to the Yankee clock trade gets its own section. The book stands as a rare insider account of how a small-state craft grew into a national industry.
14761-caxton-s-book-of-curtesye:
William Caxton's Book of Curtesye, first printed at Westminster about 1477, teaches good manners to young people entering service in a great household. Edited by Frederick J. Furnivall for the Early English Text Society, this reprint sets Caxton's text beside two manuscript copies from Oriel and Balliol colleges.

The treatise covers how to stand, speak, eat and serve without giving offence, and how to show respect to lords, ladies and fellow servants. Its rules now sound quaint, but they reveal a whole social order: rank, cleanliness, speech and table conduct as moral training. For readers of early English, the old spelling and notes make it both a conduct book and a language record.
16747-a-canadian-manor-and-its-seigneurs:
George M. Wrong, a history teacher at the University of Toronto, wrote this 1908 tale of one Canadian manor across a hundred years, 1761 to 1861. It starts with the founding of Malbaie, its first seigneurs, its burning by the British in 1759, and the Highland seigneurs who followed. Pictures and maps help place the land.

Wrong follows lords, tenants, priests, and soldiers as French rule gives way to British rule and a new Canada takes shape. The manor stands for a whole social order: land, rank, church, and kin, tested by war and change. The book gives a clear, local view of big history, told through one place and the folk who held it.
16804-an-eye-for-an-eye:
Anthony Trollope wrote this 1879 novel in two volumes, of love, promise, and ruin in Ireland and England. Fred Neville makes a promise, is called home to Scroope, and faces the Earl in trouble, while scenes shift from Ennis and Liscannor to Ardkill and the cliffs. The tale opens with a lady long shut in a private asylum in the west of England.

Trollope weighs a young man's word against his rank, his kin, and his own weak will. The lady's fixed, brooding mind haunts the whole book, a grim price for broken faith. Readers who like Trollope's moral tales will find a darker, shorter novel than his Barset books, with his usual sharp eye for class and conscience.
17164-narrative-of-a-mission-to-central-:
James Richardson's mission to Central Africa in 1850 and 1851, published in 1853 after his death, tells a British trek from Tripoli toward Lake Chad. An editor shaped Richardson's eight small journals, dispatches, and notes into this narrative. Caravan lists, camel drivers, interpreters, and trade in slaves and goods fill the early chapters, with desert marches and talks at Mourzuk and Ghat.

Richardson aimed to push lawful trade and end slave traffic, and his journal records both hope and hardship on the road. The tone is that of a field report, keen on places, prices, and peoples met. Readers of African exploration will find a frank, detailed record of a mission cut short by its leader's death.
18544-narrative-of-a-mission-to-central-:
James Richardson wrote this account of a British mission to Central Africa in 1850 and 1851, printed at London in 1853 as its second volume. Sent at government expense, the party traveled through the Sahara fringe toward Bornu, meeting sultans, traders, and desert peoples. Chapters note palaces and huts, markets, charms, meteors, and the politics of local rulers.

Fellow travelers Dr. Barth and Dr. Overweg appear often, with Barth setting out for Aghadez and news of his route reaching the camp. Richardson records vocabularies, trade in salt and agates, and the spread of Islam with a traveler's curiosity. The book remains a rich source on the Sudan before later colonial rule.
422-the-romany-rye:
George Borrow continues his wandering tale in this sequel to Lavengro, opening in a damp dingle at dawn. The narrator, camped with gypsies, mends a chaise wheel, tends his forge, and talks with Belle, Isopel Berners, and other road folk. Gypsy lore, horse deals, and sharp talk fill the roadside days.

Borrow mixes travel, language study, and picaresque jest, with long talks on books, faith, and fair play. The Romany Rye of the title names both the road and its free spirit. The book charms as a rambling portrait of England seen from the campfire, not the coach.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herve-auguste:
Hervé-Auguste-Étienne-Albans Faye was a French astronomer, born at Saint-Benoît-du-Sault in October 1814 and dead at Paris in 1902. Son of a civil engineer, he entered the École Polytechnique in 1832, left early, and joined the Paris Observatory as a pupil in 1836. There he discovered the periodic comet that bears his name in 1843, winning the Prix Lalande, and he entered the Academy of Sciences in 1847.

Faye taught geodesy at the École Polytechnique, served as rector at Nancy, and held the astronomy chair at the École Polytechnique from 1873 to 1893. He also led the Bureau des Longitudes and served briefly as minister of public instruction in 1877. His fame rests on practical and theoretical work alike, from better methods of measurement and a zenithal collimator to early uses of photography in astronomy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-de-la-ha:
Jean de La Haye, a French Franciscan Bible scholar born in Paris in 1593 and dead there in 1661. He spent his boyhood in Spain and took the habit in the Alcantarine reform. He lectured in philosophy and divinity, preached with distinction, and from 1620 held high offices in his order and at Louis XIII's court.

De La Haye authored or edited some forty folio volumes. He edited Bernardine of Siena, Francis, and Anthony of Padua, and wrote preaching commentaries on Genesis, Exodus, and Revelation. His monuments are the Biblia Magna of 1643 and the nineteen-volume Biblia Maxima of 1660, both built on the Vulgate with gathered commentaries and variant readings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sieur-de-lave:
Pierre Gaultier de Varennes, Sieur de La Vérendrye, discoverer of the Canadian West, was born at Three Rivers, Quebec, in 1685 and died at Montreal in 1749. His early manhood passed as a soldier of France, and he was wounded at Malplaquet. Returning home, he entered the fur trade. He built three posts west of Lake Superior: Fort Saint Pierre in 1731, Fort Saint Charles in 1732, and Maurepas in 1734.

A sincere Christian, he carried Jesuit chaplains with him, first Father Mesaiger, then Father Aulneau de La Touche. In June 1736 Aulneau left east with La Vérendrye's eldest son and nineteen voyageurs for provisions. The whole party was slain that very day on an island in the Lake of the Woods. He resisted native pressure to avenge the Sioux massacre. His posts' voyageur crews gave rise in time to the Métis people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-mart:
John Martin Moye was a priest of the Diocese of Metz, founder of the Sisters of Divine Providence, and missionary in China. He was born at Cutting in Lorraine on 27 January 1730 and died at Trier on 4 May 1793. Sixth of thirteen children of John Moye and Catharine Demange, he learned his first Latin from an elder brother, a seminarian, and finished his classical studies at Pont-à-Mousson's college.

Next he read philosophy at Strasburg's Jesuit college and joined Metz's theological seminary of St Simon in autumn 1751. Ordained priest on 9 March 1754, he was named vicar in the episcopal city that same month. His great zeal for souls drew attention, and many pious ladies placed themselves under his firm and wise direction. From them he chose select souls to found schools for country children, the seed of his congregation.
doe-osti-3010923-integration-and-validat: Cyber armor in layers got its DOE drill, and this text tests every stacked defense. The pages detail the RD2C results. The security folks get their method. The armor was multi-layer. The drill was DOE's. The defenses were stacked.
narrative-of-a-mission-to-central-africa:
James Richardson led a British mission into Central Africa in 1850 and 1851. Her Majesty's Government ordered and paid for the trip. Richardson had written Travels in the Great Desert of Sahara. Chapman and Hall issued this account in London in 1853.

Richardson died on the journey and left a vast journal behind. His editor shaped eight small, close-written volumes into two books. Dispatches and loose memos filled out the record. The mission crossed the Sahara toward the great lakes and Sudan. Its reports opened Central Africa to British trade and science, at the cost of its leader's life.
nasa-tm-19680026299-cylindrical-electros:
J. A. Findlay and L. H. Brace of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this July 1968 preprint, X-623-68-281, on cylindrical electrostatic probes flown on two satellites. Alouette II and Explorer 31 carried identical probe sensors into the ionosphere. Flying the same instrument on both craft gave scientists a common yardstick for comparing direct measurements between missions.

The report explains the probe theory, the sensors and electronics, and how electron temperature and density are read. Satellite differences still changed data formats and experiment voltages, the authors note. On Alouette II, the topside sounder interfered strongly with probe data. Processing that data proved difficult, they add, though not impossible.
podcast-dannyjones-ABAvPuhu9yE:
Historian Richard Dolan built his reputation on books about UFO secrecy and a possible breakaway civilization. With Danny Jones, he turns from the sky to the sea. He presents what he calls the best evidence that unknown intelligences live deep under the oceans. It is a realm he dubs an underwater Area 51.

Dolan reviews sightings of objects entering and leaving the water at impossible speeds, many from military witnesses. The ocean is the least observed part of the planet, and his argument leans on that darkness. The claims are Dolan's, offered in his measured style, and they remain unproven. Listeners who follow his work get his full underwater case in one sitting, argued by the field's best-known historian rather than its loudest voices.
podcast-joerogan-3eZnbWTb1YE:
Dakota Meyer, a Marine veteran and Medal of Honor recipient, tells Rogan about turning to ibogaine therapy for PTSD. In a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, Meyer speaks as a man who tried standard care first and kept looking when it fell short.

He describes the treatment itself, a strong psychedelic given in a clinic setting, and the shift he felt afterward. Rogan asks what the nightmares and anger were like before, and what changed after. The segment adds a first-hand voice to the wider debate over psychedelic care for veterans who carry war home with them.
the-romany-rye:
Transcribed from the 1907 J. M. Dent edition, The Romany Rye opens with a chapter headed by the making of a linch-pin, a sound sleeper, breakfast, and a postillion's departure. No author's name is printed in the pages shown.

The narrator wakes at daybreak in a dingle, lights his forge, and fashions a replacement linch-pin for a chaise wheel, copying the pin from the companion wheel. Belle watches near the forge while the postillion sleeps so soundly in the tent that the narrator jokes he must descend from one of the seven sleepers. Fitted and polished, the new pin lets them put the wheel back on.
travels-in-the-united-states-of-america-:
William Priest, a theatre musician from Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Boston, published his American travels at London in 1802. The title page dates his stay from 1793 to 1797. His journals of two Atlantic crossings form part of the book.

Priest's preface admits he wrote the account for friends after coming home in 1797. Only their urging, pressed for three months, brought it to print. He credits extracts from Jefferson, Belknap, and other American writers for much of its value. Readers get a working musician's plain view of the young United States, offered without claims to fine writing.
